# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with a fivefold increase in the risk of ischemic stroke [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention, but a substantial proportion of patients have contraindications or experience bleeding complications [2]. The left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of more than 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF, providing the anatomical rationale for percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) as a non-pharmacologic alternative [3]. This review summarizes the evidence, devices, procedural considerations, and future directions of percutaneous LAAC.

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, blind-ended structure with highly variable morphology, commonly classified as "chicken wing," "cactus," "windsock," and "cauliflower" types [4]. Non–chicken-wing morphologies have been associated with higher thromboembolic risk, underscoring the importance of preprocedural imaging [4]. Excluding the LAA from the circulation aims to reduce stroke risk while avoiding the hemorrhagic consequences of long-term anticoagulation [3,5].

## Devices and Evidence

The Watchman device (Boston Scientific) is the most extensively studied LAAC system. The pivotal PROTECT AF trial demonstrated non-inferiority of the Watchman to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in patients with non-valvular AF [6]. However, early procedural safety concerns, including pericardial effusion and device embolization, prompted the PREVAIL trial, which confirmed improved procedural safety with operator experience [7]. Long-term follow-up of these trials, including a patient-level meta-analysis, showed reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality compared with warfarin [8,9]. The Continued Access registries and the EWOLUTION registry further confirmed favorable real-world outcomes and high procedural success rates [10,11].

The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and its successor, the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott), use a "pacifier" lobe-and-disc design [12]. The Amulet IDE trial demonstrated non-inferiority of the Amulet to the Watchman for safety and effectiveness endpoints, although with a higher rate of procedural complications [13]. The next-generation Watchman FLX device improved deliverability and was evaluated in the PINNACLE FLX study, showing high closure rates with low adverse events [14].

Comparative data against direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) emerged from the PRAGUE-17 trial, which found LAAC non-inferior to DOACs for the prevention of cardiovascular events in high-risk patients [15]. These findings broadened the potential applicability of LAAC beyond patients with absolute OAC contraindications [15,16].

## Periprocedural Imaging and Antithrombotic Management

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains central to procedural planning, device sizing, and the exclusion of pre-existing LAA thrombus [17]. Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) and cardiac computed tomography are increasingly used and may reduce procedure times and contrast exposure [18,19]. Postprocedural antithrombotic regimens vary; the original protocols used warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, whereas contemporary practice often employs DOAC-based or single/dual antiplatelet strategies [20,21]. The optimal regimen, particularly in patients with bleeding contraindications, remains an area of active investigation [21].

## Complications

Procedural complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, vascular access complications, and procedure-related stroke [22]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) is a recognized late complication occurring in roughly 3–4% of patients and is associated with an increased risk of thromboembolic events [23,24]. Incomplete closure with residual peri-device leak has also been linked to adverse outcomes, although the clinical significance of small leaks remains debated [25]. Operator and center volume are important determinants of procedural safety [26].

## Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current guidelines from professional societies assign LAAC a class IIb recommendation for patients with non-valvular AF and contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [27,28]. Appropriate patient selection requires multidisciplinary evaluation, weighing thromboembolic risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) against bleeding risk (HAS-BLED) and individual anatomy [28]. Shared decision-making is emphasized given the evolving evidence base [27].

## Future Directions

Several large randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and OPTION, are evaluating LAAC against DOACs in broader populations [29]. Combined procedures, such as concomitant LAAC and catheter ablation, and refinements in device design, imaging, and antithrombotic protocols are likely to expand the role of LAAC [30]. The management of DRT and peri-device leaks, along with the durability of stroke prevention, will be clarified by ongoing research [29,30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has emerged as a valuable alternative for stroke prevention in selected patients with non-valvular AF, particularly those unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. While randomized data support its efficacy and safety relative to warfarin and, increasingly, DOACs, ongoing trials will define its place in the broader AF population.
